coherence.reasons: Both use the same four-part argument (market, unit economics, cash, software alternative) leading to the same answer, and both hold together. Y's hierarchy is tighter: it sets out four conditions the founders' case needs, gives each a verdict, and maps every section, the options table and the reopening triggers back to those tests. X has a minor internal tension. Its executive summary leads with the weaker figure (a $2.67 loss before store costs), and its comparison table shows the best-observed combination at +$0.5 because it stops before store costs. That sits awkwardly under the claim that the plan works only on inputs no site has reached, and X has to hedge with 'clearly positive only in the plan'. Y carries one consistent measure (after site costs: −$12.57, −$6.17, −$1.76, +$2.02) throughout, so its headline claim follows directly from its evidence.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (do not launch, fund the software business, sell fast delivery to grocers), and both consider and reject a one-store pilot with a cost build-up. Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It compares four options, including the status quo, on profit, runway, upside, downside and reversibility. It shows the pilot breaches the runway floor by month 6. It states the upside forgone if the founders are right (+$12M a year). It gives measurable reopening triggers tied to each test and notes Parcelbird can watch for them at no cost through its own software data. It also stress-tests its own recommendation (the floor holds down to about 34% growth, or with costs rising 10% a year) and stages the hires against bookings. X's pilot assessment is sound but thinner: it calls $4.77M left 'only just' keeping runway when that is marginally below the $4.8M floor. X also has a single reopen test and one sensitivity (40% growth), and it does candidly flag that breakeven needs about 72 contracts, twice the pipeline. Both are defensible; Y's trade-offs are more complete.

evidence.reasons: Y reproduces every required calculation: median −$6.17, best observed combined −$1.76, pop-up −$12.57, plan +$2.02, CAGR 41.5%, and $2.5M or about 6 months of runway against 12 required. Its Zipcart test gives −$1.05 per order for a median site after the 14% volume loss, which matches the key exactly. It adds valid analyses: one-at-a-time sensitivities, the week-6 pop-up run rate of about 410 a day, payback periods, and both readings of the $9.5M. It also makes the sharp point that the 14 benchmark sites already run Parcelbird software, so 'we run them better' is already in the median. It labels its own inferences (channel conflict, tranche thresholds) and the generous assumptions. X's arithmetic is also correct where I checked it (break-even AOV $46.7 before store costs, 3.8 orders per rider-hour, 1,043 orders a day with Zipcart fees, $173 per retained customer, $27.5M acquisition, $6.62M software cash use). But X mostly reports contribution before store costs. It never computes the pop-up's −$12.57 (it shows −$6.2) or the best-observed −$1.76 (it shows +$0.5), so it understates the critical evidence. X also asserts unsupported details about Zipcart ('kept the same stores and riders', 'the fix was pricing, not operations') and states the channel-conflict point as fact.

revision.reasons: Both reject the founders' hypothesis while granting the part the evidence supports, namely that market growth is real. Y handles the revision more explicitly and more fairly. It starts from the founders' 'launch' answer, lists the four things it needs to be true, and scores each (market half met, the others not met). It gives the pop-up its due (a six-week temporary site, so launch promotions and low volume are expected) and still shows the week-6 rate sits at the bottom of the benchmark range. It quantifies the Zipcart evidence that partly supports the founders: positive before site costs at +$3.02, but still −$1.05 after site costs and the volume loss. It keeps the option open with triggers. X also engages with Zipcart (+$3.02 per order, needs 1,043 orders a day) and says the founders are right about the market, and it treats the 18% weekly growth as promotion-driven. But its revision is less systematic, and it never confronts the founders' own +$2.02 figure.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the board to the right decision with broadly correct numbers. Y would serve the board better. It gives the decisive per-order figures after site costs for all four scenarios, including the pop-up and the best-observed case. It shows the plan fails the runway floor under either reading of the $9.5M. It tests the Zipcart lever through to a result. It compares four options, including a costed pilot. It stress-tests the recommended software path and gives concrete decisions, a 90-day plan and reopening triggers. X is more concise and candid about the software path's dependence on new sales, but it leans on before-store-cost figures that understate the case and offers less on sensitivity and reopening conditions. Y's extra length is used for reasoning, not padding.
